You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly show a frog placed inside the toilet bowl?
node.criteria: Pass if a frog is clearly visible within the toilet bowl; fail if the image clearly shows no frog inside the bowl; unknown if the bowl or its contents are obscured or the evidence is otherwise insufficient to determine this.
node.binding: The frog must be inside the toilet bowl of the toilet in the input image.

node_traces.evidence: A frog is clearly visible inside the toilet bowl in the edited image.

fulfillment: The node’s completion criterion is too permissive: its trace says a frog is clearly inside the bowl, but the edited image shows the prominent frog overlapping the bowl opening and existing dark object, so bowl membership is not unambiguous; other frogs are on the lid and floor. This supports progress, not confidently complete fulfillment. Tighten the completion check to require clear visual evidence that the frog is within the bowl’s interior, distinguishing it from frogs merely on the lid, rim, or nearby, and route ambiguous placement to partial/unknown rather than treating a support’s assertion as proof. Keep the partial-progress check available when completion is not established. The reference label is an aggregate constraint, not atomic ground truth; investigate the mismatch between the high-confidence yes trace and the image rather than hard-coding partial. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated: both supports were queried and valid.
s2: The node is a partial-progress support, not the completion check. Its question/criteria already distinguish a frog clearly inside the bowl (complete) from a partial attempt, but the trace appears to collapse those categories: the edited image has frogs on the lid and floor and one visibly positioned within the bowl, while the trace calls that clear progress and the aggregate is yes. Refine the typed criterion so this support reports only evidence of an incomplete attempt toward bowl placement; explicitly exclude frogs merely on the lid, rim, or nearby, and avoid counting a clearly interior frog as partial progress. Ensure the separate fulfillment check assesses whether bowl membership is visually unambiguous, routing uncertain overlap to unknown rather than inferring completion from the support’s wording. Preserve genuine partial-progress detection and do not hard-code the reference label: it constrains the aggregate, not atomic truth. The trace is valid and queried with no dependency or transport failure, so focus on criterion interpretation and routing, not schema repair. Low confidence or repeated variation should prompt evidence review, not be treated as proof that an edit is absent.
